title: The Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15)
hookLine: the first council decides Gentiles need not keep the whole Law
carry: it hath seemed good to the holy ghost

lines: MUST THEY KEEP THE WHOLE LAW?
cards: A family over a will. A parish over a building. Some arguments can split a community in two, and for the first Christians, one came fast.
Barnabas and Paul come back from their journey with news: Gentiles, non-Jews, are coming to believe.
But some believers from Judea arrive in Antioch and teach that unless the Gentiles are circumcised and keep the Law of Moses, they cannot be saved. There was, the text says, no small dissension.
So the church does something new: it goes to Jerusalem to decide together.

teach.h: A REAL QUESTION ABOUT THE LAW.
teach.b: It's worth being fair to both sides. The first believers were Jews who loved the Law.

It was God's gift to Israel, and the question was a real one: if Gentiles join the people of Israel's Messiah, shouldn't they join Israel's covenant in full? So the apostles and elders gather, and there is much disputing.
Peter stands and tells how God gave the Spirit to Gentiles at Cornelius's house, making no difference between them and us.
Barnabas and Paul tell the signs God did among the nations, and the crowd falls silent to listen.
Finally James, a leader of the Jerusalem church, speaks.
He quotes the prophet Amos about the nations seeking the Lord, and proposes a way: don't trouble the Gentiles who are turning to God.

Ask them only to keep away from food offered to idols, from blood and what is strangled, and from sexual immorality. Some readers see these as the things that let Jewish and Gentile believers share a table.
Then they write a letter, and one sentence in it carries the whole method.

teach.h: IT HATH SEEMED GOOD TO THE HOLY GHOST.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "For it hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us, to lay no further burden upon you than these necessary things." The Holy Ghost, and us.
Not one man's ruling, and not a vote cut off from prayer, but a decision the whole gathering believed the Spirit had led.
Catholics look to it as the pattern for the councils that followed, from Nicaea to the Second Vatican Council. And notice the order: they listened first, then decided.

how: The Catholic Church counts its ecumenical councils from Nicaea to the Second Vatican Council, and looks to the gathering in Acts 15 as their model; bishops still meet in synods to discern together.

o: a letter of advice from one church to another
a gathering of Church leaders deciding together
a single bishop's ruling for his own diocese

games.q: at the council — tap the pairs.
p: told of the Spirit given to Gentiles
quoted Amos and proposed a way
told the signs among the nations

s: the question at the council was a silly one
it was real: the Law was God's gift to Israel, and the first believers were Jews who loved it.
the council asked Gentiles to keep only a few necessary things
keep from idol food, blood, what is strangled, and sexual immorality.
the letter says the decision seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us
a decision the gathering believed the Spirit had led.

games.q: you're at the gathering in Jerusalem. the dispute is sharp and loud. what do you do?
o: decide quickly before it gets worse.
let each side tell what God has done, and listen.
games.why: Peter, then Barnabas and Paul, tell what they've seen, the crowd goes silent to listen, and James proposes a way the whole gathering accepts.

practice: Think of a decision you're facing that involves other people, at home, at work, in a group you belong to, and ask who hasn't been heard yet.

Picture them speaking, the way the whole crowd went quiet to hear Paul and Barnabas, and let the question sit a moment before you answer it. If you pray, ask for the Holy Spirit's help before you decide.

wordCard.voice: Council. The apostles and elders gathered in Jerusalem, listening, arguing, and deciding together what seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to them. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: it seemed good. the word Greek cities used to open their public decrees, here used of the Holy Ghost and the apostles.

carryVoice: Your line: it hath seemed good to the holy ghost. Tomorrow, a riverbank outside Philippi. Day five hundred forty-eight, done.
